newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan coffee roasters find it hard to raise prices.
newsitem.headline: Japan coffee roasters find it hard to raise prices.

text.p: Japan's coffee roasters, hit hard by surging world coffee prices and the weaker yen, are having a tough time convincing retailers to swallow higher wholesale prices, Japanese roasters and traders said on Thursday.
"Although we're facing very tough circumstances, we can't raise prices as easily as U.S. and European roasters can," an official of the All Japan Coffee Association said.
He said most suppliers of regular coffee were small companies that face cut-throat price competition and stiff resistance from big, powerful retailers.
"We are trying to persuade end-users to accept higher prices, but I can't tell at this stage by what percentage prices can be raised," an official at a leading roaster said.
The plight of Japanese suppliers was in marked contrast to the situation in Europe, where retail prices were recently raised 20 percent in response to a rally in world prices.

On New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, prices raced to their highest level in nearly two-and-a-half years on Wednesday, sailing through the widely watched $2 a lb mark. Prices have risen 75 percent since the beginning of the year.
Japan's instant coffee roasters were in a better position, traders said, as that market is dominated by two large suppliers.

After a rally in 1995 sparked by frosts in Brazil, Japan's retail prices for instant coffee were raised by an average of 12 percent, and some sources suggested a double-digit hike was likely again in the current rally.
Japanese traders also said world coffee prices have more scope to rise, backed by strong fundamentals, while any technical correction could be short-lived.
"There may be some correction as the speed of the recent price gains was too rapid, but the fundamentally bullish tone remains intact," a source at a major trading house said.
"World coffee consumption has increased while global coffee inventories are low. Near-term supplies are especially tight," he said.
